title: CORS browser origins preflight and credential policy
concepts: CORS is a browser-enforced response-sharing protocol, not server authentication or a general firewall. The same-origin policy blocks many cross-origin reads; CORS lets a server opt origins into access.

Simple cross-origin requests may be sent before the browser checks response-sharing headers; non-simple requests trigger a preflight OPTIONS exchange. Request permission and response visibility are distinct.

Credentialed CORS requires an explicit allowed origin and credentials permission; wildcard origin is incompatible with credentialed response sharing. CORS does not stop non-browser clients or direct requests.
An origin is scheme, host, and port. Compare normalized origins exactly; unsafe substring or suffix matching can admit hostile domains.

CORS is not server-to-server access control

The Fetch Standard is a living standard; CORS safelists, preflight processing, credential behavior, redirect handling, and cache rules must be checked against the current text rather than treated as a frozen API snapshot.
